Adverb of Degree — very, quite, nearly, entirely and partly. (Answers the question HOW MUCH?)
Interrogative Adverbs — when, where, how and why.
CLAUSE
Noun clause — Does the work of a noun in a complex sentence.
Subject of the verb: What she says is quite true. That he is an honest man is quite clear. Why she left is a mystery.
Object of the verb: I do not know when she will come. Tell me why you told a lie.
Object of a preposition: Pay careful attention to what he says. He was greatly pleased with what I said. No one knows how old she is.
Complement of a verb of incomplete predication: Her fear is that she may fail. Life is what we make of it. His belief is that ghosts can talk.
Apposition to a noun or pronoun: My hope is that you may pass. It is clear that he was innocent. The report that he was killed is false.

Adjective clause — It is introduced by a relative pronoun or relative adverb.
This is the boy who won the first prize. This is the house that John built. The time when the train leaves is not known. The reason why he told a lie is not known.
Adverb Clause
Adverb Clause of time — Introduced by subordinating conjunctions — when, whenever, while, before, after, since, till, as etc.

When the cat is away the mice are at play. He goes mad whenever he comes to visit his mother’s grave. Do not talk while you are eating. Before you leave switch off the light. I have been ill since you have left. As soon as the train had left, my friend rushed into the platform. No sooner did he see me than he took to his heels.
Adverb Clause of place — Introduced by subordinating conjunctions — where, wherever, whenever.
I have kept the book where no one can find it. Wherever he goes follow him. You can come whenever you like.
Adverb Clause of purpose — Introduced by subordinating conjunctions — because, as, then, that and since.
I am glad because you are in time. I am glad that you do not like it. I am glad since you promise to serve me faithfully. I am glad as the truth comes out.
Adverb Clause of condition — Introduced by subordinating conjunctions — if, whether and unless.
If it rains we shall not play. He will not pass whether he works or not. Unless he works very hard he will fail.
Adverb clause of Result — Introduced by subordinating conjunctions — so.
He is so old that he can hardly work. She is so kind a woman that all respect her. The news is so good that it cannot be true.
Adverb Clause of comparison
Degree: She is younger than she looks. He is as foolish as he is lazy. He is not as wise as you think. Manner: She does as she pleases. As you sow, you will reap. It all ended as we expected.
Adverb Clause of supposition or contrast — Introduced by subordinating conjunctions — though, even though, although etc.
Though he is fair, she hates him. Although he was ill, he attended the class. Even if he is old, he is able to do a lot of work.
PREPOSITIONS
A preposition is a word placed before a noun or pronoun to show what relation the person or thing denoted by the noun stands to something else.
There is a cow in the field. He is fond of tea.
Kinds of prepositions
Simple prepositions: At, by, for, off, in, with, on, out, to, through, from…
Compound prepositions: According, above, about, along, amidst, among, around, behind, beside, between, inside, outside, underneath, within, without.
Phrase prepositions & phrasal verbs: According to, in addition to, in place of, along with, in case of, in regard to, because of, in course of, in spite of, by dint of, in favour of, instead of.
The uses of at and in
At is used for a point of time as — He came here at day break, at sunset etc. At is also used with reference to space, for small towns, villages — I met him at Keeranur. I will see him at school.
In is used for a period of time in which something happens — in the morning, in the month of May, etc. In is also used for big towns, cities, countries — He works in Mumbai. He works in Dubai.

ARTICLES
Observe these sentences
Arjunan fought like a hero.
I saw an elephant yesterday.
This is the camera you gave me.
a, an, and the are called Articles. Their function in any statement or sentence is purely grammatical.
Indefinite article: a, an. Definite article: the.
The indefinite article “a” is used before: Noun beginning with the sound of a consonant.
A boy, a flower, a woman, a cow, a horse. Such words as have the sound of (Y).
A useless person, a ewe, a European, a unit, a utensil, a unicorn, a union, a university. Nouns beginning with (O) though a vowel, but with the sound (WO).
A one rupee note, a one way road, a one eyed giant, such a one.

The indefinite article “a/an” is also used:
Idiomatically — a few, a little.
In figurative expressions — few, little.
Before numerical expressions — a lot, a thousand, a dozen.
In expressions of price, speed, ratio — 50 kms an hour, three times a day and Rs.100 a meter.
In exclamations before singular countable nouns — What a hot day! What a pretty baby!
With a noun complement, including names of professions — He is a Teacher. She is a dancer. I am an engineer.
